item.title: AI should only run as fast as we can catch up
item.description:
However, to make AI work actually useful (not only works, but reliable and trustworthy), we also need to catch up with what the AI does as quickly as possible. If verification ~= learning/creation, one spends equal amount of time checking AI’s work. “Does this look right.

HN Discussion

Read Original Article

Top 7 Comments:

jascha_eng:

Verification is key, and the issue is that almost all AI generated code looks plausible so just reading the code is usually not enough. You need to build extremely good testing systems and actually run through the scenarios that you want to ensure work to be confident in the results. This can be preview deployments or other AI generated end to end tests that produce video output that you can watch or just a very good test suite with guard rails.

Without such automation and guard rails, AI generated code eventually becomes a burden on your team because you simply can't manually verify every scenario.

blauditore:

All these engineers who claim to write most code through AI - I wonder what kind of codebase that is. I keep on trying, but it always ends up producing superficially okay-looking code, but getting nuances wrong. Also fails to fix them (just changes random stuff) if pointed to said nuances.

I work on a large product with two decades of accumulated legacy, maybe that's the problem. I can see though how generating and editing a simple greenfield web frontend project could work much better, as long as actual complexity is low.

cons0le:

I directly asked gemini how to get world peace. It said the world should prioritize addressing climate change, inequality, and discrimination. Yeah - we're not gonna do any of that shit. So I don't know what the point of "superintelligent" AI is if we aren't going to even listen to it for the basic big picture stuff. Any sort of "utopia" that people imagine AI bringing is doomed to fail because we already can't cooperate without AI

yannyu:

I think there's a lot of utility to current AI tools, but it's also clear we're in a very unsettled phase of this technology. We likely won't see for years where the technology lands in terms of capability or the changes that will be made to society and industry to accommodate.

Somewhat unfortunately, the sheer amount of money being poured into AI means that it's being forced upon many of us, even if we didn't want it. Which results in a stark, vast gap like the author is describing, where things are moving so fast that it can feel like we may never have time to catch up.

And what's even worse, because of this industry and individuals are now trying to have the tool correct and moderate itself, which intuitively seems wrong from both a technical and societal standpoint.

CGMthrowaway:

> AI should only run as fast as we can catch up

Good principle. This is exactly why we research vaccines and bioweapons side by side in the labs, for example.

gradus_ad:

The proliferation of nondeterministically generated code is here to stay. Part of our response must be more dynamic, more comprehensive and more realistic workload simulation and testing frameworks.

rogerkirkness:

Appealing, but this is coming from someone smart/thoughtful. No offence to 'rest of world', but I think that most people have felt this way for years. And realistically in a year, there won't be any people who can keep up.

item.title: Microsoft has a problem: nobody wants to buy or use its shoddy AI products
item.description:

Based on reports that Google Gemini is now actively beating ChatGPT's best models, FirstPageSage has Google Gemini sprinting past Microsoft Copilot quarter over quarter, although ChatGPT itself will remain the front runner. Google Gemini in Google Apps is also far smarter and far more intuitive than Copilot on Microsoft 365, as someone actively using both.

Everything it currently stands on is a legacy product with roots in the Ballmer or Gates eras. They owe their Azure footprint and "success" today to Ballmer.

Their inability to produce anything useful with Copilot is the largest example of this, but there are others. They are getting lapped by a ~300 person software company in the race to consumer-ize an x86 PC a into turnkey gaming platform, even with $100 billion in game studios and owning the API that every major game is developed against. Their footprint in education is gone, completely replaced by Google who not only produced an operating system that could be effectively run and managed on commodity hardware, but also developed the centralized functions for school administrations to use to manage classrooms at scale.

The consumer situation for Microsoft right now might be even worse than it was when Nadella took over.

The sudden demand for sub-$500 laptops during the pandemic showed him that people still liked Windows and wanted a good OS from Microsoft. But instead of capitalizing on it to give customers what they wanted, he just gave us an ad-filled spyware with AI slop.

item.title: A series of tricks and techniques I learned doing tiny GLSL demos
item.description:
Let's simplify the problem with the following figure: A ray passing by a radiating object The glowing object sends photons that spread all around it. The further we go from the object, the more spread these photons are, basically following the inverse square law 1/r^2, which gives the photons density, where r is the distance to the target object. Given two arbitrary sampling points and their corresponding distance d_n and d_{n+1}, any intermediate distance can be linearly interpolated with r=\mathrm{mix}(d_n,d_{n+1},t) where t is within [0,1].

item.title: RIP Tetsu Yamauchi (Former Free and Faces Bassist)
item.description:
Tetsu Yamauchi onstage with the Faces in 1973 (Image credit: Ian Dickson/Redferns) Tetsu Yamauchi, former bassist with Free and the Faces, has died at the age of 79. item.description:

There are not many industries where it’s more valuable to stop selling bits and start selling atoms, but every major creator eventually pivots to selling products because it’s more lucrative than chasing views and brand deals.
